criteria.detail: The three statements of the truncation literature, read back on a machine lasting up to 8 periods with a declining output profile. **The truncation that maximises the wage is the one chosen at every rate probed**, and **at that truncation every old-machine price is non-negative**, and **it is the longest truncation of which that is true**. Read at rates 0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.9: r=0.00 gives life 6 and longest non-negative truncation 6; r=0.20 gives life 7 and longest non-negative truncation 7; r=0.50 gives life 8 and longest non-negative truncation 8; r=0.90 gives life 8 and longest non-negative truncation 8. **The fourth statement in that literature is that the economic life varies with the rate of profit, in either direction depending on the example**, and this carrier shows the variation, with the direction reported in B78-6c as this carrier gives it rather than as a general claim
criteria.name: B78-5
criteria.statement: the truncation results of the fixed-capital literature, read back

criteria.detail: The economic life read off `max_T w_T(r)` at 400 rates from 0 to 0.95, for four output profiles. **Each truncation is a technique and the life is the owner of their envelope**, so everything B76 proved about envelopes applies to it without a new argument. **The life moves with the rate**: declining gives [6, 7, 8] over 388 viable rates of 400; constant gives [8] over 311 viable rates of 400; rising gives [8] over 234 viable rates of 400; humped gives [6, 7, 8] over 298 viable rates of 400. **Rates at which no truncation is viable are excluded rather than counted as a change**, which is what the first prototype got wrong: its sentinel for an infeasible rate read as one more fall
criteria.name: B78-6a
criteria.statement: Theorem 23(1): the economic life is the owner of the wage envelope over truncations

criteria.detail: The same sweep, with the two characterisations compared **at every viable rate rather than at a few spot values**. **The truncation that maximises the wage is exactly the longest one whose own old-machine prices are all non-negative**, on 1231 of 1231 rates across the four profiles: declining 388 of 388; constant 311 of 311; rising 234 of 234; humped 298 of 298. Both halves are checked separately: **the chosen truncation passes the price test on all 1231**, and **no longer truncation ever passes it**, 0 of 1231. **Each truncation must be asked about its own price system.** Reading the first negative age off the untruncated system instead is off by one and agrees only on 1044 of these 1231 rates; four spot rates did not catch it and a dense sweep did
criteria.name: B78-6b
criteria.statement: Theorem 23(2): the wage-maximising truncation and the first negative price are the same age

criteria.detail: **How often the economic life can change as the rate runs is bounded by B76's bound on an envelope with `k` members**, here `2k - 2 = 14` for `k = 8` candidate truncations. The four named profiles change 2/0/0/2 times, and 120 drawn profiles reach at most 3, owner sequence [5, 6, 7, 8]. **The life can skip an age**: yes, [5, 7, 8]. **On the direction this carrier is one-sided**: across the drawn profiles the life rises with the rate 47 times and falls 0 times. **That is reported as what this carrier gives, not as a general claim**: the literature's examples show both directions and non-monotone cases, and nothing in the construction fixes a direction, because the life is an envelope owner and owner sequences are governed by the crossing structure rather than by any monotonicity
criteria.name: B78-6c
criteria.statement: Theorem 23(3): how often the life changes, whether it skips, and which way it goes

criteria.detail: With the process count held at 6, **each machine age costs exactly one cycle and each land quality costs none**, and **the two do not interact**: `b_1` reads 0 ages and 0 lands give 6, 0 ages and 3 lands give 6, 1 ages and 0 lands give 7, 1 ages and 3 lands give 7, 2 ages and 0 lands give 8, 2 ages and 3 lands give 8, 3 ages and 0 lands give 9, 3 ages and 3 lands give 9, 4 ages and 0 lands give 10, 4 ages and 3 lands give 10. An age position is delivered by one process and bought by the next, so its degree is two; a land under extensive rent is bought by one process only, so its degree is one. **One machine age and one land with two users give the same `b_1`, 7 against a base of 6**, while a land with one user leaves the base untouched. **So fixed capital and intensive rent are the same graph move and extensive rent is the other one**, which is B72's Corollary 17.1 recognised in a construction that corollary was not about. **The extra cycle per age is the extra machine price to determine**
criteria.name: B78-6d
criteria.statement: Theorem 23(4): an age costs one cycle, a land costs none, and an age is a land with two users

mapping.B78-5: read back -> PASS; not read back -> FAIL, and the code or the reading of the source is fixed first
mapping.B78-6: every check holds -> PASS; any check fails -> FAIL, and the code is fixed. These read no data and decide nothing about the world
